opening.headline: We cover why “think step by step,” which works well in general models, is not helpful in inference models, and how to instruct inference models.
body: In order to help people solve math problems, prompts that worked well in the general model are often used in the inference model. If the solution order was determined by number and the results turned out to be rather awkward, it is not that the technique was wrong, but that the nature of the model was different.

The inference model thinks internally before writing a response. In this class, we will look at how the internal reasoning affects the instruction method and determine which general model techniques are valid and which are unnecessary. At the end, we compare the two directive amendments and establish criteria to determine which is appropriate.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain instruction methods suitable for inference models
You can distinguish between techniques that are effective for general models and those that are unnecessary for inference models.
You can determine whether an instruction amendment is appropriate.

screens.title: When I added “Think step by step,” the quality dropped.
screens.lead: Read both prompts side by side and look at the explanation on the right. Compare what changes were made to the same problem and what the results were.

visual.alt: A two-pronged scene in which a simple prompt leads to a stable answer, and a prompt that forces a procedure leads to an awkward answer.
labels: Please tell me the answer and rationale for this math problem.
Think step by step, solve in the following order: step 1 formula, step 2 calculation, step 3 verification.

data.code:
[Existing Prompt]
Tell me the answer and rationale for this math problem.

[Edited prompt]
Think step by step: Step 1 is setting up the equation, Step 2 is the calculation.
Step 3 is to solve in verification order.

[Result]
Existing prompt: Stable answer
Edited prompt: The flow has become unnatural and errors have increased.

notes.note: This prompt simply states your goal. When the inference model receives this request, it internally creates a plan and reviews the solution, resulting in a stable answer.
This prompt is a direct copy of a technique that worked well in the general model. Forcing step numbers can conflict with the model's own plan and make the solution flow awkward.

The OpenAI Inference Model Guide explains that instructions like “think step by step” do not increase performance and can sometimes hinder it. The question we will answer in this lesson is what is the inference model doing inside that makes procedural instructions an obstacle?

screens.outro: Let me start by recalling my own experience.

screens.title: Have you ever copied the techniques for regular models?
screens.lead: As you select each technique, the instructor's thoughts unfold. First think about what techniques you have used and then press it. You will not enter or submit an answer.

items.answer: This is the most widely used technique in general models. This is a method to increase accuracy by having the model write down its thinking process. But the inference model already does this internally. So adding the same phrase duplicates the internal reasoning and has little effect.

items.prompt: Technique: “Explain the solution process in detail.”
items.answer: Instructions requiring explanations are meaningful if the purpose is for human review of the results. However, if the goal is to increase the correct answer rate, it is unnecessary for the inference model. The same phrase has different uses depending on the purpose.

The more examples a general model has, the better it follows the format. The inference model guide tells you to first try without examples and add decimals only when necessary. Even if you use an example, it should be very close to the instructions.

This is a useful habit in general models where the order of operations is important. The strength of an inferential model is its planning, so forcing an order would limit its power. This is the central question of this lesson.

screens.outro: Now let's start by checking what the inference model does before responding.

screens.title: Inference models think within first
screens.lead: Select each tab to see how the three providers explain their reasoning. The final tab organizes commonalities.

visual.alt: A flowchart where input goes through the thinking steps inside the model and comes out as a response.
labels: The token used here is an inference token.

tabs.label: OpenAI
tabs.body: According to OpenAI documentation, the inference model uses an internal inference token before creating a response. During this process, the model makes plans, explores alternatives, and resolves ambiguities. The OpenAI guide likens these models to planners, and the fast and inexpensive GPT model to workhorses. The inference model is good at solving problems where planning is important, but the GPT model is suitable for quickly processing a given task.

tabs.label: Gemini
tabs.body: Gemini's mental model is to reason internally before responding. The API shows this internal process as a thought step, which contains a signature and an optional summary. Tokens written in thought are also separately counted as `total_thought_tokens` in response usage. By default, the Gemini model dynamically adjusts its inference effort based on the complexity of the request.

tabs.label: Claude
tabs.body: Claude's thinking is adaptive. The model decides whether or not to think about each request and how deeply. You can set an intent and specify effort if needed, and the model will distribute the inferences where they will be helpful. This method works well for a mix of easy and difficult requests.

tabs.label: common ground
tabs.body: All three providers already have internal inferences made before responding. This reduces the need for prompts to explicitly write procedures. What the model needs is not a solution, but what it wants and the constraints it must adhere to. The heart of the inference model instructions lies here.

screens.outro: Now that you understand the internal reasoning, let's break down what the guide recommends and what it doesn't.

screens.title: Recommended and Not Recommended: A Guide to Inference Model Prompts
screens.lead: Read the table to check which instructions the guide recommends and which instructions he does not recommend, along with the reasons. The last line is the most important point in this lesson.

data.caption: Dos and Don'ts of Inference Model Prompts
rows: This is because the inference model is strong at understanding intent even in short instructions and filling in gaps on its own.
Divide input areas with delimiters such as markdown, XML tags, or section titles.
If you make it clear which part of the input is data and which is an instruction, the model will have less trouble interpreting it.
Try without examples first and add a few examples only when necessary.
The examples must match the instructions very closely, as any deviation may result in poor quality.
Specify constraints to be adhered to, such as “budget under $500”
This is to inform the model of its boundaries so that it does not guess the constraints just by looking at the goal.
Encourage thought processes such as “Think step by step” or “Explain why”
This is unnecessary, does not increase performance, and is sometimes intrusive since it is already inferred internally.
data.notes: Recommendations are all about informing the model of your goals and boundaries. What is not recommended is forcing the model to use a solution method. In other words, the direction of the guide is to tell us what you want, but leave it up to you how to solve it. By comparing each row of the table with your own prompt, you'll quickly see where you need to make corrections.

screens.outro: Next, we will see how goal-focused instruction and reasoning strength are linked.

screens.title: Goal-focused instruction and reasoning strength
screens.lead: Move the slider to change the strength of your inference. Depending on the value, the description of depth of thought and speed of response varies. Goal-driven instruction remains the same at any intensity.

visual.alt: Illustration showing the relationship between the reasoning strength slider, depth of thought, and response delay.
labels: The instructions remain the same, only the intensity is adjusted.

stops.body: Think lightly and respond quickly. It's suitable for simple questions or formatted conversions and saves tokens. The lower OpenAI's `reasoning.effort` also leans toward speed and token savings. The goal-oriented instruction “Find the final amount and state your assumptions in one line” can be used in this intensity as well.

This is a good intermediate step for common problems. The Gemini model basically thinks dynamically based on requests and can be specified as low, medium, or high with `thinking_level`. For most tasks, it is better to start with this level and adjust after seeing the results.

Think deeper and consider more alternatives. It is used when accuracy is required in difficult multi-step problems, which results in slower responses and more tokens. Claude's effort is a gentle guide that adjusts the aggressiveness and depth of your thoughts in five levels: max, xhigh, high, medium, and low.

You can write "don't think" when you want to think less, but Claude's guide tells you to lower effort before the prompt. It is cleanest to leave depth to settings and goals and constraints to prompts.

screens.outro: Now that you know the principles, let's move on to an explanation that will help you identify unnecessary techniques.

screens.title: Commentary: Sorting out unnecessary ones among general model techniques
screens.lead: Select the right arrow to follow the instructor as he breaks down the techniques one by one. Each technique is assessed as either maintained, reduced, or unnecessary.

steps.title: “Think step by step”: unnecessary
steps.body: Inference models already think step by step internally. Remove this phrase because it duplicates the internal reasoning, making it ineffective and making the flow awkward.

steps.title: “Constraints are explicit”: maintained
steps.body: Constraints that must be maintained, such as budget or rounding standards, remain in effect in the inference model. Rather, when simply writing down the goal, the clearer the constraints, the more stable the results.

steps.title: "Split input by delimiter": keep
steps.body: The guide recommends dividing the input area with markdown or XML tags. The effect of preventing mixing of data and instructions is effective regardless of model type.

steps.title: “Attach multiple examples”: abbreviation
steps.body: Try without examples first and add a few examples only if necessary. When writing examples, align the instructions and shapes so that they do not conflict with each other.

steps.title: “Force the solution order by number”: shortened
steps.body: Reduce it as it can hinder the model's planning ability. If there is an order that must be followed, write it down briefly as a constraint and leave the rest to the model's planning.

steps.title: Organize classification results
steps.body: Among the five techniques, there is one to delete, two to reduce, and two to maintain. There is only one criterion for judgment. The question is, does the technique tell the model what it wants, or does it instead decide how the model will solve it? Keep what comes before and reduce what comes after. Knowing these criteria allows you to classify techniques you see for the first time in the same way.

screens.outro: Now that we've sorted out the techniques, let's compare the two instructions and judge for ourselves.

screens.title: Commentary: Comparison of instructions that only give goals and instructions that force procedures
screens.lead: Alternate between the two instructions and compare your instructor's evaluation notes. The problem is a cost calculation problem, and the goal is to find the final amount.

states.label: Instruction A: Enforcing Procedure
states.body: “Be sure to solve the problem in the following order: Step 1 variable definition, Step 2 formula, Step 3 calculation, Step 4 verification.” In this instruction, the solution order is numbered. In terms of evaluation criteria, the goal is not clear. There is no word on finding the final amount, no constraints are specified, and procedural enforcement remains. They are inappropriate for inference models because they are instructions that limit their planning capabilities. Moreover, because the verification steps are numbered, the model will remain within this framework even if a better verification method is found.

states.label: Instruction B: Goal-focused
states.body: “Find the final amount and state on one line the assumptions used. Rounding is done to the nearest Korean won.” These instructions only give the desired results and constraints and leave the solving procedure to the model. Goals are clear, constraints are stated, and there is no forced process. Having the assumptions stated in one line is a way to obtain a basis for reviewing the results instead of determining the solution order, so it is suitable for an inference model. Even if the results are wrong, it is easy to correct because you can check in one line which assumption was off. Comparing the two instructions, three evaluation criteria become apparent. Are the goals clear, are the constraints stated, and are the procedures left to enforce?

screens.outro: Now that we have confirmed the three criteria for judging amendments, let us close by summarizing the main points.

screens.title: Key takeaway: Give goals and constraints and leave the process up to you.
screens.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class. Try to answer the question we posed at the beginning: what is the inference model doing inside that makes procedural instructions an obstacle?

paragraphs: Inference models plan internally and explore alternatives before responding. So, adding “Think step by step” means re-doing what you’re already doing, and forcing the solution order by number conflicts with the model’s plan. The reason why procedural instructions are an obstacle is not because the model is bad, but because it interferes with what the model is already doing well.

So the focus of direction is on goals and constraints. Prompts are simple and direct, constraints to be followed are clearly written, and input areas are divided into markdown or tags. Try without examples first, and when necessary, add only a few as instructed.

The depth of your thoughts is controlled by the strength of your reasoning, not by your phrases. OpenAI's `reasoning.effort`, Gemini's `thinking_level`, and Claude's effort play that role. When evaluating an amendment, you can check in turn whether the goal is clear, whether restrictions are specified, and whether procedural enforcement remains.

Going back to the original example, modifications that number steps to a math problem are filtered out for remaining procedural constraints in this check. This check can be used as is whenever you move a prompt for a generic model to an inference model. When moving to a new model, it is a good idea to first check to see if any instructions need to be removed rather than added. Short, clear prompts are the most reliable starting point for inference models.

callout.label: Inspection criteria
callout.text: Are the goals clear, are the constraints specified, and are there any procedures left to enforce? Evaluate directive amendments using three questions:

glossary.def: It is a directive style that is simple, direct, and clear in its goals and constraints.
Instructions that force a solution sequence or encourage step-by-step thinking. In inferential models, this may be ineffective or disruptive.
This is an instruction that writes down the desired result and the constraints that must be observed, and leaves the solution method to the model.
This setting controls how deeply the model thinks. These include OpenAI's reasoning.effort, Gemini's thinking_level, and Claude's effort.

misconceptions.myth: The more detailed the procedure, the better the inference model solves it.
misconceptions.fact: Inference models plan themselves internally, so forcing a process can be disruptive. It is better to have clear goals and constraints.

misconceptions.myth: Inference models should be given many examples.
misconceptions.fact: Try without examples first, and only when necessary add a few examples consistent with the instructions. If the examples do not match the instructions, the quality may deteriorate.

misconceptions.myth: To reduce thinking, simply write “don’t think” as a prompt.
misconceptions.fact: It is more stable to control depth by inference strength rather than phrases. Lower the effort first, then adjust the wording.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: We give the inference model a goal and constraints and leave the procedure to it.
Prompts like “think about it step by step” overlap with internal reasoning and are unnecessary or intrusive.
Delimiters and explicit constraints remain valid in inference models as well.
The depth of your thoughts is controlled by the strength of your reasoning, not by your phrases.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: Which part of my prompt is forcing a solution process?

checks.q: I'm trying to get my inference model to solve a math problem. What prompt modifications are appropriate for the direction of the guide?
options: The order from step 1 variable definition to step 4 verification is enforced by number.
Add ‘Think step by step’ to each sentence to encourage inference.
Teach the solution method first by attaching at least ten examples.
Write simply and directly only the final results and the constraints that must be adhered to.
checks.explain: Because the inference model already makes inferences internally before responding, it is best to keep your prompts brief and direct, specifying your goals and constraints.

wrong.0: Procedural enforcement can hinder a model's planning ability.
wrong.1: Step-by-step guided thought overlaps with internal reasoning and does not increase performance.
wrong.2: For examples, try without first and add decimals only when necessary.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. When you select one of the views, a commentary appears. Results are not recorded.

checks.q: Match the following terms and descriptions
right: A method that determines the solution order into steps 1 and 2
The process by which a model plans and considers alternatives before responding.
A method of writing only the desired results and constraints and leaving it to the model to solve them
Settings that control how actively and deeply you think.
checks.explain: Goal-centered only determines results and constraints, while process-centered determines the order. Effort is a setting that adjusts the depth of your thoughts.
checks.intro: Organize terms by pairing concepts with explanations. Results are not recorded.

checks.q: In the cost calculation problem, instruction B is 'Find the final amount and state in one line the assumptions used. Rounding is to the nearest Korean won. Why do you think B is better suited to the inference model?
options: This is because the goals and constraints are clear and the solution procedure is left to the model.
This is because every solution step is assigned a number to prevent errors.
This is because inference is reduced because a separate verification step is not required.
This is because the instruction sentences are short and no inference tokens are generated.
checks.explain: B is an instruction that fits the inference model, specifying goals and constraints and leaving the procedure to the model.

wrong.1: Enforcing procedures by number is a feature of Instruction A.
wrong.2: The criterion is not whether the inspection is conducted, but whether the procedure is enforced.
wrong.3: Inference tokens arise as internal inferences regardless of instruction length.
